title: Astro Bob: Rise early on Oct. 22 to see meteors from Halley's Comet
excerpt: The annual Orionid meteor shower will be active all week and peak Thursday morning.
content:
Every October, Earth crosses the orbit of Halley's Comet, and we're pelted with its dusty debris. Sand-grain-sized bits of rock boiled off the comet during its repeated passages of the sun spread out along its orbit like a contrail behind a jet plane. Traveling at 18 1/2 miles a second, Earth slams into the material, and it strikes our atmosphere at around 148,000 miles per hour.

Even a sand grain possesses a hefty amount of energy at that speed. It compresses and heats the air in its path, which strips away its atoms and transforms the air around it into a narrow streak of glowing plasma we see as a meteor flash. All this happens in a fraction of a second. Simple physics, right? But there's something miraculous about seeing how a comet that typically only passes through our neighborhood once every 76 years shows up every year, albeit transformed into meteors that make our hearts leap.

The Orionids aren't as numerous as the Perseids of August or December's Geminids, but they're reliable. During peak activity, which occurs Wednesday night, October 21-22, about 20 meteors per hour are visible from a dark, moonless sky. They emerge from a point (called the radiant) in the upraised club of Orion about a fist above the bright, ruby star Betelgeuse. Halley's debris is headed in our direction, so Earth strikes the material nearly head on, the reason Orionids zip past so fast.

For the best view of any meteor shower the radiant should be as high in the sky as possible, otherwise you'll only see meteors shooting upward. The rest are hidden below the horizon. Orion rises around 11 p.m. Normally, you could start watching the shower around midnight-1 a.m. But this year a bright, waxing gibbous moon washes out the sky until it sets around 3-3:30 a.m. That leaves 3 hours of rock solid, dark-sky viewing until the start of dawn.

I like to watch the shower just outside of the city where the sky is much darker. You'll see the brightest ones nearer town, but in most showers, fainter "shooting stars" dominate. If you're willing and able to drive, go for it. You'll see more meteors. Watching is simple and straightforward. All you need are your eyes and a folding lounge chair. Bring a wool blanket or sleeping bag to cover up. A wool cap and insulated boots will keep you cozy.

Halley-ids originate from one spot but they stream anywhere and everywhere across the sky. If you're out around 4 a.m. look to the east-southeast or west-northwest. With Orion off to one side of your view you'll see an assortment of short- and long-trailed meteors.

Being outside in the wee hours you'll get to see and hear things most of us sleep through — the winter stars and winter Milky Way, great-horned owls, Jupiter and Mars climbing up the eastern sky and the gentle clatter of brittle leaves in the breeze. Enjoy!

"Astro" Bob King is a freelance writer and retired photographer for the Duluth News Tribune. You can reach him at nightsky55@gmail.com.
